asSun.p: Aquarius has two rulers, depending on who you ask. The older astrologers gave it Saturn, the modern ones added Uranus once it was discovered, and most Aquarius Suns recognise both in themselves, the part that likes rules and the part that likes breaking them. The Star is Aquarius's card. Look at her pouring water out of two jugs, which is the water-bearer doing the sign's own job, and with your Sun in Aquarius the card is yours. The awkward bit is that the Sun is in detriment here. Aquarius sits opposite Leo, where the Sun is at home, so its wish to be the centre of attention has to work against the grain. You still want to shine. You just want to do it on behalf of something, a group, an idea, a better way of running things, and you get uncomfortable when it's only about you. Aquarius is fixed air, so the ideas stick. Once you've made up your mind about something, you tend to hold that view for decades.

It comes out as a sort of friendly stubbornness. You'll agree with nearly everyone in a meeting and then quietly do it your own way, and you're mildly surprised when people are cross about that. At a family lunch you're the one asking why everyone has to go to your aunt's every Easter, and you actually want an answer. Someone at work makes a joke that punches down and you don't laugh, and everyone notices you not laughing. You're often right about things years before they catch on, and you can be a bit insufferable about it in the meantime. You also keep odd friendships going for ages, the ex-colleague in Berlin, the neighbour from three houses ago, a group chat that's mostly you sending articles. Being liked matters to you. You're a little embarrassed that it does.

You're fair to people you don't much like. The Sun's discomfort in Aquarius actually helps here, because a Sun that isn't set on being the centre doesn't need every argument won by you personally. So you can hear a good idea from someone who annoys you and say so in front of everyone. In a planning meeting you'll back a junior colleague's proposal over your own, without any fuss, because theirs was better, and people remember that for years. You're also quick with strangers in trouble. The woman whose car's broken down, the lost kid at the footy, the new person at the club standing on their own. You're over there before most people have registered it, and you don't need to know them first.

You can care about people in general so well that the particular ones miss out. You'll spend a Saturday at a working bee for the community garden and forget to ring your mum back about her test results. There's also a contrary streak tied up with who you think you are. If everyone likes a thing you're already a bit suspicious of it, and if a friend agrees with you too quickly you'll sometimes shift your position just to keep a little distance. That's the detriment showing. With the Sun uneasy in this sign, fitting in can feel like vanishing, so you hang on to what makes you different, and after a while it gets lonely. And when someone tells you you've hurt them, you go straight to explaining your reasoning, and they end up feeling they've been argued with.

Trouble tends to turn into a cause. A redundancy becomes a question about how the company treats everyone it let go, and by the evening you're drafting the email to HR and reading up on employment law. You sound calm on the phone, and people take the calm at face value. Give it a week and you're still at it, still reasonable, and you've stopped answering anyone who wants to talk about how you feel. Your partner wanted to talk about the mortgage and got a lecture on workplace rights. Fixed air holds a position, and under strain the position is usually 'I'm fine, I've thought it through'. You'll discuss the problem for hours and never quite say you're scared. What actually helps is someone who asks what you want out of this, for yourself, and waits through the bit about principle until you answer.

You fall for people partly for what they stand for. Someone can be funny and good-looking and great company, and if they're rude to a waiter or shrug at the things you care about, you go off them fairly quickly. That's fair enough. The harder part is the Sun's unease in this sign, which makes being adored strangely hard to sit through. A partner who's proud of you in public, who gives the speech at your fortieth, can make you squirm and change the subject, and they notice that. You can also be so busy being reasonable that you forget to be romantic. Say the soppy thing now and then. Book the dinner. On your birthday, let them make a fuss of you and don't deflect it.

Work has to be for something. You can put up with a dull job for a while if you believe in what the organisation's doing, and you'll be miserable in a well-paid one you think is pointless. The Sun's detriment shows up at work as an uneasy relationship with credit. You want your ideas to win, and you don't want to be seen chasing a promotion, so you undersell yourself at review time and then feel quietly hard done by. You're good at systems, at spotting that the whole team is doing something the long way round, and at getting a room of very different people to pull together on one project. Hierarchy is harder. A manager who says 'because I said so' loses you inside a month. Look for places flat enough that a good idea can come from anywhere.

At twenty an Aquarius Sun usually has a cause, often several, and a strong opinion about how everyone else is living. You can be quite hard on people who don't think the way you do, and you're lonelier than you let on. At that age you want to be seen and would hate anyone to catch you wanting it. By the mid-thirties most have found their people, a group, a movement, a workplace, a band of friends, and the edges soften because you don't have to prove you're different any more. You get more practical about change too. The fifties tend to be good years. The Saturn side of the sign comes forward, you become the person who actually knows how the committee works, and younger people bring you their unlikely plans because you won't laugh at them.

Once this week, when someone asks what you think, give your own preference before your principle. 'I'd like Thai' before 'well, it depends what everyone wants'. 'I missed you' before 'it makes sense to catch up'. It'll feel oddly exposing, as if you've taken up too much room. Do it three times over the week and notice who looks pleased.

asMoon.p: The Moon has no special dignity in Aquarius. It's a visitor there, neither helped nor held back, so it takes a lot of its colour from the sign's ruler, Saturn in the old system and Uranus in the modern one. Saturn gives your feelings some reserve and a bit of discipline. Uranus makes them arrive in sudden shifts, nothing for days and then all at once. The Star is Aquarius's card, and with your Moon there it describes what you need in order to feel safe. Aquarius's natural house is the eleventh, friends and groups and the people you've chosen, and that's often where an Aquarius Moon finds its safety, which can be a sore point with family. The sign is fixed as well, so once a feeling has properly settled in you, it takes a long while to shift.

You tend to think a feeling before you feel it. Someone says something unkind at a barbecue and you're halfway through working out why they said it before you notice you're hurt. A friend cries on the phone and you're good with them, really good, and then you hang up and need an hour of quiet with nobody talking. A Sunday with nothing planned is often bliss for you, a long walk and a podcast and no obligations, where other people would feel lonely. You need your own room, or at least your own corner, and your own time to go to bed. Too much closeness at once, a week of houseguests, a partner who wants to talk through every mood, and you start to feel oddly airless. Then something small happens, a kind message from someone you barely know, and you're moved out of all proportion.

Other people's moods don't flood you. When your housemate's in a foul temper or your teenager slams a door, you can notice it, leave it with them, and get on with dinner, and that's rarer than you'd think. It means people can be difficult around you without being punished for it. You're also a good friend to people who are a bit odd or out of step, because you never needed anyone to be normal to feel comfortable with them. I've seen an Aquarius Moon be the one person a very shy colleague would eat lunch with, every day for a year. And you keep up with people over long gaps. Three years without speaking and you pick up where you left off, with no guilt on either side.

Your need for space can look like not needing anyone at all, and after a while you start believing that yourself. You ask for help later than you should, usually after the thing's already sorted. A partner asks what's wrong and you say you're just tired, and you mean it, because you genuinely haven't looked yet. The Saturn colouring can make you strict with your own feelings, as if some of them are allowed and some are a bit embarrassing. Jealousy, neediness, missing someone, those go in a drawer. And because Aquarius is fixed, an old hurt can harden into a principle. You stop going to the family Christmas and say it's about the politics, when really it's about one thing your dad said in 2014.

Stress sends you straight into your head. Grief, a job loss, a friend's betrayal, and you're piecing together exactly what went wrong and when, or reorganising the spare room at midnight. You'll tell people what happened in a very level voice. The feeling usually comes through a few days later, somewhere strange, halfway through a film or at a stranger's kindness in a shop, and it can knock you flat for an afternoon. With Uranus colouring this Moon, the waves tend to come suddenly. The people around you can feel locked out in that first stretch, and they sometimes back off, thinking you want them to, which leaves you alone longer than is good for you. The best help is company that doesn't ask questions. Someone on the other end of the couch, a friend to walk beside, a meal cooked for you.

You need to be able to breathe in a relationship. It sounds colder written down than it is. You love someone better when you're allowed to miss them, and a partner who texts all day or wants every evening together can leave you feeling hemmed in, however much you care about them. The relationships that last are the ones where you actually like each other on an ordinary Tuesday. You show affection in slightly unusual ways. You'll remember the exact tea they like, fix their bike, send them a photo of a dog that looks like them at two in the morning. Tell them that's what it is. They may not work it out on their own, and a partner whose feelings run hot and loud can read your quiet as a lack of love.

You need some autonomy to feel safe at work. Being micromanaged gets under your skin physically, and an open-plan office with no quiet corner tires you in a way that's hard to explain. Working from home often suits you far better than it suits your colleagues. You're steady with upset clients and panicking teammates, because you don't catch the panic, which makes you good to have around in a crisis or in any job that deals with people on their worst days. The catch is that you can seem unbothered when you're actually rattled, so managers underestimate what a restructure or a clash with someone has cost you. Tell them. And sort out the quiet you need before you're worn out, a day at home, a desk away from the kitchen, headphones everyone understands.

Around twenty an Aquarius Moon often feels like the odd one out, in the family especially, and has learnt to keep feelings at arm's length because that was the safe option at home. Through the thirties there's usually a reckoning with closeness. A relationship or a child asks you to be available in a way that doesn't come naturally, and you find, sometimes to your surprise, that you can do it on your own terms. The Saturn side helps here, because it gives you staying power. By the fifties most have a settled, unfussy emotional life, a few deep friendships, plenty of warm acquaintances, and a calm that other people find restful. The risk later on is getting set in your solitude, so that a weekend with the grandkids or a friend who comes to stay starts to feel like an invasion.

Next time you catch yourself explaining a feeling instead of having it, stop and name it in one word, out loud or on paper. Hurt. Lonely. Jealous. Relieved. Don't add the reason, just the word. Then, if someone's with you, tell them the word and let them respond before you add any context. It's uncomfortable the first few times, and it does get easier.

asRising.p: With Aquarius rising, Saturn is your chart ruler, with Uranus alongside it if you use the modern rulers, and The Star, as Aquarius's card, is the one people meet first. Aquarius was coming up over the eastern horizon when you were born, which puts it on the first house, your body, your manner, the way you go into things. Saturn at the front of a chart gives a certain reserve, a slightly formal, self-contained way of holding yourself, and Uranus adds a flash of something unexpected. Most people with this rising have both, and you can see them switch. Aquarius is fixed air, so the manner holds steady over the years. People who haven't seen you in a decade tend to say you haven't changed a bit, and they mean the way you carry yourself as much as your face.

People often say they couldn't read you at first. At a new job you're friendly to everyone in the first week and nobody can tell who you actually like. At a party you'll talk to the person no one else is talking to, have a long, odd conversation about train timetables or fungi, and leave without saying goodbye. Your style is usually a bit off to one side. It might be one strange piece of jewellery with an otherwise plain outfit, or the same black jumper every day for years. When you walk into a room you look around it before you commit to a corner. Strangers tell you surprising things on buses and in queues, because you look like you won't judge them. And you start projects in a sudden burst, then go quiet while you work out the structure.

You put people on an equal footing without meaning to. Your manner doesn't change with status, so the cleaner and the chair of the board both get the same interested, slightly detached attention, and both of them tend to like you for it. That makes you good in rooms where there's a power imbalance, a parent-teacher interview, a job interview with a nervous candidate, someone's first day. The other gift is that your instincts about where things are heading are often early. You'll say a café won't last, or a colleague's about to leave, or a friend's relationship has run its course, and a few months on it turns out you had it. You often can't say how you knew. Uranus, your chart's modern co-ruler, tends to work in flashes like that, and the reasons usually catch up a few weeks later.

The reserve that makes you easy to trust can also make you hard to reach. People take the cool first impression as the whole story, and you let them, because correcting it would mean showing more than you'd like. At work drinks you'll be pleasant to everyone for two hours and come home having told no one a single real thing. Saturn ruling the chart can put a guardedness into the body itself, the folded arms, the slightly stiff way of sitting, and people read that as judgement when it's actually nerves. There's also a habit of reacting against whatever's expected of you in the moment. Someone tells you to calm down and you get sharper. Someone assumes you'll go along with the plan and suddenly you've got objections you didn't have five minutes ago.

When something goes badly wrong, your manner gets flatter and more controlled. A car accident, a hard phone call from the hospital, a public row at work, and you're the person who goes very still and starts giving practical instructions. Saturn, your chart ruler, is good at that. People around you feel steadied and a little unnerved at once, because you've shown no feeling at all. The body collects later, often a week or two on. Stiff neck, bad sleep, restless legs, or a sudden urge to change something big, quit the job, cut your hair off, move house. That's Uranus wanting out. Friends can be startled by the swing from calm to drastic, and a bit hurt that they didn't see it coming. Exercise that properly tires you out helps, and so does one person you'll admit to that you've been shaken.

With Aquarius rising, Leo falls on your seventh house, the house of partners. So the people you're drawn to are often big-hearted and a little theatrical, happy to take the spotlight, generous in a way that seems a bit much at first. Being around them teaches you to enjoy some attention, which doesn't come easily with your reserve. The early stages can be tricky. You come across as friendly and detached, and a potential partner often can't tell whether you're interested, so tell them. Taurus sits on your fourth house, home, which means that behind the front door you want things stable, comfortable and a bit old-fashioned, good food, a proper bed, routines that don't change. That surprises people who fell for the unconventional first impression, usually in a good way.

Scorpio is on your tenth house, career and public standing, so however breezy you look, your working life tends to be intense and fairly private. You're often drawn to work that goes deep, research, investigation, therapy, finance, anything where you get to find out what's really going on. In interviews you come across as calm and quietly original, and people remember you afterwards. Colleagues see someone easygoing, then watch you refuse to budge on something you think matters, and it throws them. You get trusted with confidential things fairly quickly, the draft budget, the complaint nobody else is meant to see. The risk is that nobody knows what you want from your own career, because you've never said. Tell the person who decides, in plain words, before the next round of changes.

At twenty Aquarius rising often looks older and cooler than it feels. You might have been the kid who dressed strangely, or the one everyone thought didn't care, and a lot of that was shyness in disguise. Through the thirties the Saturn side starts to pay off. The reserve gets read as reliability, and you're the one handed the keys, the rota, the client nobody else can manage. The unexpected streak doesn't go away, and it often shows up as one big change somewhere in that decade that no one saw coming. By the fifties the look usually settles into something distinctive and unmistakably yours, and the reserve eases. You're often the one who crosses the room to say hello at a party, which would have surprised you at twenty.

At the next gathering where you know hardly anyone, tell the first person you speak to one true thing about yourself inside five minutes. Something small, like the fact that you nearly didn't come, or that you've had a strange week. Watch what it does to the conversation. Your reserve does a useful job most of the time, and it's worth knowing what happens when you put it down for ten minutes.

asBirthCard.p: This card comes from your birthdate, and it has nothing to do with where your Sun or Moon happen to sit. Add up every digit of the date, and if the total goes over 22, add its digits again. You landed on 17, which is The Star. Seventeen is a one and a seven, and those add up to eight, which is Strength's number. People tend to miss that. The card looks gentle, a woman pouring water out under the night sky, and there's something tough underneath it. Then look at where it sits. Card 16 is The Tower, the lightning strike and the collapse. Card 18 is The Moon, the confusing night where nothing is clear. The Star is the quiet stretch in between. The card's own astrology is Aquarius, fixed air, ruled by Saturn and in modern astrology by Uranus as well, and that's where it gets its long view and its oddly steady hope.

As a pattern across a life, 17 tends to show up as a run of rebuilding. Something falls down, your parents split when you're a kid, a business goes under, a move to a new city goes badly, and you find yourself in the aftermath doing the quiet work of starting again. You might notice you've been the one who organised the meal roster when a friend's partner died, or kept the friends together after the big falling-out. At work people come to you after the merger, when everyone else is sulking. Your own hard times seem to come in the same shape. A shock, a bad few months, then a slow and slightly surprising recovery that leaves you better off than before. After a few rounds of it you start to trust the pattern, a bit.

You're hard to shame about your own low points. Because you've come back from things before, you can talk about the divorce or the breakdown or the year you were broke without much embarrassment, and that gives other people permission to talk about theirs. I've watched someone with this birth card mention, over a work lunch, that they'd once been sacked, and within ten minutes the whole table was swapping stories they'd never told. You're also patient with slow things, a garden, a friendship that's taking years to thaw, a skill you're still rubbish at after three years of lessons, and you keep turning up without needing a result.

You can get comfortable in the aftermath. If you've spent a lot of your life rebuilding, calm can start to feel suspicious, and some people with this card quietly go looking for the next thing to fix. A friend in crisis, a partner who needs rescuing, a failing project at work you volunteer for when your plate's already full. You can also hand out hope to others that you won't give yourself. You'll tell a mate that losing their job is the start of something, and in the same week call your own setback proof that you always mess things up. A lot of people with 17 spend good years braced for the next blow when nothing's coming, and the people who love them find that tiring.

When the bottom falls out, you get practical and a little too cheerful. You make lists, ring around, reassure everyone, including the people who should be reassuring you. Then the next card in the sequence often turns up, a week or so later, the foggy, anxious Moon stretch where you can't sleep and everything looks worse at 3 a.m. You don't tell many people about that part, because you're known as the hopeful one and it feels wrong to fall apart. So the people around you get a slightly brittle version of you and can't work out why. Rest has to come before the plans. Sleep, food, a day off, and one person who knows you well enough to say you don't have to be the optimist this time.

You tend to fall for people who'll admit they're scared, and polish on its own leaves you cold. You're very open early on, which some partners find disarming and others find too much too soon. A lot of people with this card meet their important partners during or just after a hard stretch, and the relationship carries some of that feeling of recovery in it. That can be lovely. It can also mean you stay in the role of healer long after the other person's healed. Keep checking that there's still room for you to be the one who's struggling. And let yourself be pleased when it's going well. Some of you wait for the other shoe to drop, and a partner can feel that.

The pattern suits work where things get put back together. Nursing, rehab, counselling, rescuing a failing shop, teaching kids who've had a rough start, restoring old furniture, disaster recovery. You're steadiest in the part of the job everyone else finds depressing, the long middle where nothing looks better yet. The Aquarian streak in the card itself shows up as an interest in fairness and in how things could be organised better, so you may end up on the working group or pushing to change how the shifts are done. The danger is becoming the team's permanent morale officer. When the office leans on you to keep spirits up, it's fine to say you're tired, and fine to let someone else bring the cake.

In the twenties this card often shows up as a first real collapse and a first real recovery, a degree abandoned, a big relationship ending, a move that doesn't work, and the discovery that you come back. It's also when a lot of people with 17 are at their most idealistic and most easily let down. By the mid-thirties most have been through the cycle two or three times and stopped being surprised by it. The hope gets sturdier and less naive, and you start to be the one others seek out after their own Tower moment. The fifties usually bring a more settled version. Fewer storms, or maybe you just see them coming earlier, and a strong wish to pass on what you've learnt, to kids, to a younger colleague, to anyone starting over.

Keep a short list somewhere private of the times you came back from something. The job you lost and the one that followed. The breakup and who you became afterwards. The illness, the move, the year that went wrong. Just a line each. When the next bad stretch arrives, read it before you decide what the setback says about you. Add to it as the years go on.
